Case Study — Fintech / Payments

Redesigning Pay on Credit: diagnosing a 97% drop-off, then designing against evidence

Housing.com's credit-card bill-pay flow was losing 97 of every 100 users who started it. A funnel analysis paired with a structured heuristic evaluation isolated four concrete, fixable failure points across two screens — the resulting redesign recovered 224 completed payments a day and ₹3.36 crore in monthly transaction volume.

1Context

What Pay on Credit does

Pay on Credit is a financial product built inside the Housing.com app that lets users pay high-value obligations — house rent, tuition fees, and similar recurring bills that are traditionally settled in cash or by bank transfer — using a credit card instead. The value proposition is straightforward: pay what you owe with credit you already have, without needing liquid cash on hand.

It competes in a category that already has entrenched players, CRED and CreQ among them. For a challenger product, credibility and low friction aren't nice-to-haves — they decide whether a user with alternatives already installed on their phone stays through checkout or bounces to a competitor.

2My Role

Owning diagnosis through delivery

As the Principal Product Designer on this project, I owned the end-to-end design of the Pay on Credit experience — from diagnosing why the funnel was leaking users to shipping the final redesigned screens.

I worked with Product Managers to align on business priorities and define what success looked like, and partnered directly with Data Analysts to interpret the funnel telemetry and confirm which drop-off points represented the biggest, most solvable opportunities before committing design time to them.

3The Problem

A 97% failure rate on a flow designed to build trust

Every day, over 20,000 users entered the Pay on Credit journey. Only 3 in 100 completed a payment. For a product whose entire pitch is "trust us with your credit card for a high-value bill," a 97% failure rate meant the interface itself — not a lack of user intent — was the primary blocker standing between demand and revenue.

4Research & Diagnostic Methodology

Diagnose before designing

Rather than redesigning from intuition, I anchored the diagnosis in two evidence-based methods, run in parallel, so every design decision downstream could be traced back to a measured "where" and a diagnosed "why."

Method 01

Quantitative Behavioral Analysis

Working with the data team, I mapped the complete session-level funnel — from a user selecting "Pay on Credit" from the Housing.com home screen through PAN verification, card entry, and payment completion — and quantified the drop-off at every single node. This turned a vague "conversion is low" complaint into a ranked, specific list of exactly where and how severely users were leaving.

Method 02

Heuristic Evaluation

Independently of the funnel numbers, I audited every screen in the three-step payment flow against established usability heuristics — visibility of system status, match between system and the real world, error prevention, recognition over recall, and trust & credibility cues. This identified the specific interface decisions that were plausible causes for the drop-off the funnel had already located.

The full funnel, instrumented end-to-end: 20,241 daily sessions enter at the landing page; by the time the flow reaches the Pay CTA, the vast majority have already left. Each labelled arrow (48%, 18%, 10%, 1%, 8%, 4%) is a measured drop-off, not an estimate — this is what let the team rank problems by size of opportunity rather than by opinion.

Two things stood out immediately in the payment-steps portion of the funnel (Step 1: Enter Amount → Step 2: Beneficiary Details → Step 3: Receiver's Name): the Amount screen and the combined Beneficiary Details / Name screens accounted for the largest, most concentrated, and most fixable share of the loss inside the actual payment flow the design team controlled — as opposed to upstream steps like login or PAN verification, which were shared infrastructure outside this project's scope. That's where the heuristic evaluation was pointed next.

5Findings

Four diagnosed failure points

The heuristic evaluation, cross-referenced against the funnel data, surfaced four specific problems across two screens. Each is presented here with the interface evidence, the heuristic it violates, and the drop-off it's associated with.

Problem 01 & 02 — Amount Screen 34% drop-off

No clear entry point, and a non-actionable offers section competing for attention

Violates: aesthetic & minimalist design   Visibility of system status

The single most critical action on the screen — entering an amount — had no visual weight or direction: a bare underline, no label prominence, no placeholder guidance. Meanwhile, a ₹9,999 "Jackpot" offer occupied more screen real estate than the input itself, despite having no CTA a user could actually tap. Users landed on the screen with no obvious starting point, while the most visually dominant element on it did nothing.

Impact
Hesitation before the transaction even begins, and attention pulled away from the one action that matters at this step.
Problem 03 — Beneficiary Details Screen 25% drop-off

Credentials requested without context

Violates: trust & credibility   Visibility of system status

Users were asked for sensitive bank information — account number, confirmation, IFSC code — with no copy explaining why it was needed, how it would be used, or whether it would be stored. A user who arrived intending to pay by credit card was suddenly asked for bank credentials mid-flow, with no warning.

Impact
Distrust-driven abandonment at exactly the point the product most needed to feel safe.
Problem 04 — Final Step Screen 24% drop-off

Unnecessary input at the finish line

Violates: recognition over recall   Flexibility & efficiency of use

At Step 3 of 3, users were asked to manually type their name — information almost certainly already available from their account profile. Adding a manual input at the point of highest intent interrupted momentum and implied the platform didn't already know who they were.

Impact
Friction introduced immediately before payment, the single worst place in the flow to add it.
6Goals & Success Criteria

What "solved" needed to mean, defined before designing

Business goals

Improve conversion across the payment journey. The flow was losing users at every stage, with only 3% completing a payment. Success meant reducing drop-off at each step and increasing daily completed transactions — a direct revenue lever.

Compete credibly in the credit-payments market. With CRED and CreQ already established, Pay on Credit needed to be trustworthy and seamless enough to retain users who had alternatives one tap away.

User goals

Reduce friction and give users a clear next step. Simplify the journey, cut unnecessary clicks, and remove any step that didn't directly serve payment completion.

Build trust at every stage. Introduce the right trust signals at the right moments — particularly at high-anxiety points like credential entry and final confirmation — so users felt safe enough to complete the transaction.

7From Diagnosis to Hypotheses

Every design decision started as a testable claim

Before touching the interface, each diagnosed problem was reframed as an if/then/because hypothesis. This is what kept the redesign accountable to evidence rather than taste — every solution below exists to test one of these six claims.

H1

If the amount input becomes the single, unmistakable focal point of the screen and the non-actionable offers carousel is removed, then completion of Step 1 will increase,

because users act faster when one obvious action replaces several competing, ambiguous stimuli.

Addresses Problem 01→ Solutions 1 & 3
H2

If mandatory consent is surfaced as its own explicit, timed moment instead of a passive checkbox next to the primary CTA, then consent will be reliably captured without adding a perceived extra step,

because visibility of a required action increases compliance without increasing effort.

Addresses Problem 02→ Solution 2
H3

If the category-switch action is demoted from a header-level control to an inline, secondary affordance, then it will stop competing visually with the primary task,

because an edge-case action should carry proportionally less visual weight than the primary conversion path.

Supports Problem 01→ Solution 4
H4

If the confirmed amount stays pinned throughout the flow and every new field is clearly labelled before it's requested, then trust-driven abandonment during credential entry will decrease,

because context reduces the perceived risk of an unexplained request.

Addresses Problem 03→ Solution 5
H5

If UPI — the method most users already pay with — is pre-selected as the default, and a verified beneficiary name confirms the recipient inline, then abandonment driven by uncertainty will decrease,

because removing a discovery step and confirming correctness both lower perceived risk before commitment.

Addresses Problem 03→ Solutions 6 & 7
H6

If the name field is relocated into a contextual, optional section within the same screen instead of appearing as a surprise mandatory field at the last step, then late-stage abandonment will decrease,

because a request feels lower-friction when it's part of a logical grouping rather than an unexplained new ask.

Addresses Problem 04→ Solution 8
8Design Solutions

Two screens, rebuilt against the hypotheses

The three-step flow was also restructured at a higher level: Steps 2 and 3 — previously separate screens for bank/UPI details and the receiver's name — were consolidated into a single Beneficiary Details screen with a progressive, accordion-based layout. That alone removed an entire step from the journey before any individual field was touched.

Screen 1 — Amount Entry

Testing H1, H2 and H3. Baseline drop-off: 34%.
Solutions 1–4
Solution 1 · Tests H1

Prominent and focused amount input

The amount input is now the undisputed hero of the screen — large, centred, with the rupee symbol as the first thing users see, and quick-select chips for common amounts sitting directly below.

RationaleUsers land with one clear job: enter an amount, with no ambiguity about where to start.
Solution 2 · Tests H2

Terms and conditions given their own moment

Consent was previously buried in the same visual space as the primary CTA, with no indication it was mandatory. It's now surfaced as a dedicated undertaking that appears automatically after a short delay.

RationaleUsers no longer miss or skip consent — its mandatory nature is communicated clearly before they can proceed.
Solution 3 · Tests H1

Offers section removed

The non-actionable Jackpot carousel — previously the most visually dominant element on the screen — was removed entirely.

RationaleThe screen now serves exactly one purpose: capturing the payment amount.
Before: a bare input competing with a non-actionable offer banner. After: the amount is the only thing on screen worth looking at, and consent surfaces as its own explicit step rather than a buried checkbox.
Solution 4 · Tests H3

Category selection simplified

The "Change Category" action was previously a header-level control competing for attention. It moved to a simple inline dropdown below the amount chips — accessible, but no longer prominent.

RationaleAn edge-case action no longer competes visually with the primary task.
Before: category switching lived in the header, next to the back button, at the same visual weight as navigation. After: it's a secondary, inline "Switch category" affordance.

Screen 2 — Beneficiary Details

Testing H4, H5 and H6. Combines what were previously Steps 2 and 3.
Solutions 5–8
Solution 5 · Tests H4

Context before input

The confirmed amount now stays pinned at the top of the screen throughout the flow, and the input section is explicitly labelled "Beneficiary Details" — telling users exactly what's being collected before they type anything.

RationaleUsers no longer feel blindsided by a credential request appearing mid-flow.
Solution 6 · Tests H5

UPI as the default selection

The screen now defaults to UPI ID — how the majority of users actually pay — with Bank Transfer available as a secondary option, instead of requiring users to discover or switch tabs.

RationaleMost users reach the right input immediately, with no extra steps required.
Solution 7 · Tests H5

Inline UPI verification

Once a UPI ID is entered, the verified beneficiary name now appears inline with a green "Verified" badge before the user taps Next.

RationaleUsers get confirmation they're paying the right person before committing, reducing abandonment driven by uncertainty.
Before: an unexplained bank-details form. After: a labelled, context-first screen defaulting to UPI, with inline verification of the recipient's name before the user commits.
Solution 8 · Tests H6

Name field retained, but contextualised

The name input is no longer an orphaned field on a separate final screen. It now sits inside an "Other Details" section within the same Beneficiary Details screen — clearly part of a logical grouping rather than an unexpected ask at the last step.

RationaleThe input feels purposeful and in context, rather than arbitrary — reducing the friction of being asked for information at the wrong moment.
Before: a surprise required field at Step 3 of 3. After: the same field, now inside an optional, clearly-grouped "Other Details" section on the consolidated screen.
9Validation & Results

What actually moved, and how confident to be about why

How this was measured

Impact was measured through a before/after comparison of production funnel metrics across comparable time windows immediately before and after launch — not a randomized, controlled A/B test with a held-out control group. That's a meaningful caveat: sequential before/after comparisons can be influenced by seasonality, concurrent marketing pushes, or other changes shipped in the same window, so the numbers below should be read as strong directional evidence rather than a controlled causal proof. Where possible, the shift was cross-checked against the step-level funnel to confirm recovered users were tracking through to completed payments rather than simply moving the drop-off point further downstream. A natural next step — covered in Reflection below — is running this class of change through a proper A/B test.

Combined business impact

Together, the two interventions translated into 224 additional completed payments per day — a 32% absolute lift on a baseline of 701 daily transactions.

10Reflection & What's Next

The two biggest, most fixable leaks — not the only ones

This phase targeted the largest concentrated drop-off inside the payment flow the design team directly controlled. The same funnel that surfaced those two screens also shows meaningfully sized leaks upstream and downstream that remain open:

48%
Landing / category-selection page to the payment steps — the single largest leak in the entire funnel, sitting outside this phase's scope.
Not yet redesigned
8%
Beneficiary PAN verification step, immediately after Beneficiary Details.
Not yet redesigned
4%
Credit card details entry to the final Pay CTA.
Not yet redesigned

I'd also want to close the methodological gap in how the next round gets validated. Sequential before/after comparisons are a reasonable way to move fast, but they can't fully separate the effect of a redesign from seasonality or other changes shipped in the same window. Running the next set of changes as a proper controlled A/B test — with a held-out control group — would let the team attribute lift to the design decision itself with meaningfully more confidence, and is the change I'd prioritize before tackling the 48% landing-page leak, which is large enough that getting the read on causality right matters.

Pay on Credit — Housing.com. Case study by Kaif Saleem, Principal Product Designer.
